title: Design a URL Shortener
subtitle: Build the whole system: create a short link, redirect fast from a cache, and count clicks without slowing anyone down.
learn: Why a shortener is a read-heavy system and how the 100:1 ratio shapes every choice
Three ways to generate short keys and why block allocation from a counter wins
How a cache-aside redirect path serves most traffic without touching the database
Why click analytics go through a queue instead of the redirect path
How to size traffic, storage, and cache with simple back-of-envelope numbers

steps.title: Two jobs, very different load
steps.body: A URL shortener does two things: turn a long URL into a short one (a write), and turn the short one back into a redirect (a read). Assume 100 million new links a month, which is about 40 writes per second. People click far more than they create, say 100 clicks per link, so reads run near 4,000 per second on average and maybe 12,000 at peak. Those are assumptions, but the shape is real: reads dominate.
steps.idea: Design for the read path first; the write path is small and can afford to be slower.
steps.caption: Two paths share one store: rare writes, constant reads.

steps.title: Create a short link
steps.body: The client sends POST /links with the long URL. The load balancer hands it to a create service, which validates the URL (scheme, length, not on a blocklist) and picks the short key. It then stores one row mapping key to long URL, plus the owner and an optional expiry. At 40 writes per second the write rate is trivial; it is the 3 TB of total storage, covered at the end, that eventually forces sharding by key.
steps.idea: Writes are low volume, so correctness (unique keys, valid URLs) matters more than raw speed here.
steps.caption: A POST reaches the create service.

steps.title: Generating the short key
steps.body: A 7-character key from 62 symbols (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) gives 62^7, about 3.5 trillion keys. Hashing the URL and truncating, or picking random keys, risks collisions you must detect and retry. A better way: the create service asks a key allocator for a block of numbers, say 1 million, and hands them out locally as a counter, encoded in base62. No per-write coordination, no collisions by construction. Start the counter at 62^6 (or pad) so every key is exactly 7 characters. The allocator persists one counter durably (a database row or a consensus store); it is called once per million links, so it is no bottleneck, and servers keep issuing from their current block while it is briefly down.
steps.idea: Allocating ID blocks from a counter avoids collisions and makes key creation a local, constant-time step.
steps.caption: Once per million links, the create service leases a block; every other write is local.

steps.title: Sequential keys leak
steps.body: Plain counters give keys that are guessable and enumerable: anyone can walk through links one by one. If you do not want links walked in order, scramble the number before encoding, for example with format-preserving encryption, so output looks random but stays unique. With billions of 7-character keys in use, random guessing still finds live links, so scrambling is not access control. If a leased block is lost in a crash, you skip those numbers; gaps cost nothing.
steps.idea: A counter plus a reversible scramble keeps keys unique and stops people walking them in order, but short keys are still guessable, so truly private links need auth or long random tokens.
steps.caption: The allocator only hands out blocks, never single keys.

steps.title: A redirect, served from cache
steps.body: Someone opens short.example/aZ3kQ9x. The redirect service looks the key up in Redis first. For popular links this is a hit: a sub-millisecond lookup returns the long URL, and the service answers with an HTTP redirect. Link popularity is heavily skewed, so assume the hottest few percent of keys serve about 90 percent of reads, so a modest cache absorbs most traffic. Cache-aside means the app, not the cache, loads missing entries.
steps.idea: A small cache in front of the store absorbs almost all redirect traffic.
steps.caption: Cache hit at peak load: redirect returned without touching the database.

steps.title: A cache miss falls to the store
steps.body: A rarely used link is not in Redis. The redirect service reads the row from the URL store by primary key, a single indexed lookup that takes a few milliseconds, then writes the result back to the cache with a TTL so the next click is a hit. Keys that do not exist are cached briefly too, so a flood of bad or tombstone/expired keys cannot hammer the database.
steps.idea: Misses cost one indexed read plus a cache fill; negative caching protects the store from junk keys.
steps.caption: Miss: read from the store, then refill the cache.

steps.title: 301 or 302?
steps.body: A 301 says the move is permanent. Browsers cache it by default, which cuts load but hides later clicks from your analytics and makes edits slow to take effect. A 302 (temporary) is sent every time, so you keep counting and can change the target. Services that need accurate stats or editable targets usually send a 302 (or 307). Some send a 301 and accept less accurate counts; 301 with Cache-Control: no-store behaves differently, but most teams just use 302. On edit or delete, the service removes the cache key, and the cache TTL is capped by the link's expiry, so changes and expired links stop redirecting quickly.
steps.idea: The redirect status code decides whether you keep control and visibility, or save load.
steps.caption: A 302 forces every click back through the service.

steps.title: Count clicks off the hot path
steps.body: Writing a count to the database on every redirect would turn 12,000 reads per second into 12,000 writes per second. Instead, the redirect service drops a small event (key, time, country) onto a queue and returns immediately. A worker takes batches and upserts one row per (key, minute, country) with an idempotent write, since queues deliver at least once. In production this usually goes to a separate analytics store, drawn here as the same database to keep the diagram small. Counts lag by seconds.
steps.idea: Fire-and-forget events plus batch aggregation keep analytics from slowing redirects.
steps.caption: Click events flow through a queue to a batching worker.

steps.title: The cache goes cold
steps.body: Suppose the Redis cluster restarts and every key is gone. All 12,000 reads per second now miss and land on the store, and the store sized for about 1,200 reads/s may fall over. Latency spikes. Defences: replicate the cache, warm it from recent hot keys before taking traffic, coalesce concurrent misses for the same key into one database read, add jitter to TTLs so keys do not expire together, and shed or rate-limit load while it warms.
steps.idea: A cache that hides load also hides your real capacity, so plan for the day it is empty.
steps.caption: Cold cache: nearly every redirect hits the database.

steps.title: Numbers that hold it together
steps.body: Napkin math: 100 million links a month for 5 years is 6 billion rows; at about 500 bytes each that is roughly 3 TB, so shard by key or use a store that scales out. Link traffic is concentrated on recent links; if the hottest 1 to 2 percent of the 6B keys (60 to 120M keys at about 200 bytes) serve about 90 percent of reads, that is only about 12 to 24 GB, so a small Redis cluster is enough. Blocks of IDs make writes cheap, cache-aside makes reads cheap, and queues keep analytics out of the way.
steps.idea: Read-heavy design: cache the hot keys, allocate IDs in blocks, and push counting off the critical path.
steps.caption: Healthy again at average load: 90 percent of reads never reach the store.

quiz.q: Why does a block-allocation counter beat hashing the long URL to make short keys?
options: Hashes cannot be encoded in base62
Each key is unique by construction, so there are no collisions to detect and retry
Counters produce shorter keys than any hash
Hashing requires a separate database per key
quiz.why: Handing out numbers from leased blocks guarantees uniqueness without checks. Truncated hashes can collide and need retry logic.

quiz.q: After you switch redirects from 302 to 301, the click counts on your dashboard drop sharply, while the destination sites report unchanged visitor numbers. What is the most likely cause?
options: Analytics workers crashed at the same moment
Browsers cache the 301, so repeat clicks never reach your service
quiz.why: A 301 is permanent and cacheable, so browsers skip your service on repeat visits and those clicks are never counted.

quiz.q: The cache has a 90 percent hit rate at 12,000 reads/s. Roughly how many reads per second reach the database, and what does a cache restart do?
options: About 1,200; load jumps toward 12,000 until the cache warms
About 12,000 always; the cache only saves latency
quiz.why: 10 percent of 12,000 is 1,200 misses. With an empty cache nearly every read misses, so the store suddenly sees up to ten times its normal load.

quiz.q: Why send click events through a queue instead of incrementing a counter in the database during each redirect?
options: Queues guarantee the exact count in real time
It keeps a slow or contended write off the redirect path and lets a worker batch updates
It removes the need for a cache
quiz.why: Redirect latency should not depend on a write. Queueing decouples the two and batching turns thousands of tiny updates into few larger ones.

cheatsheet.def: Assume about 100 reads per write. It tells you to optimise redirects and cache hard, and keep creation simple.
7 base62 characters give 62^7, about 3.5 trillion keys. 6 characters give 56 billion, which is enough for many systems.
Servers lease ranges of IDs (for example 1M at a time) and encode them locally. Crashes only waste unused numbers.
On a read, check the cache, on a miss read the store and fill the cache. Add TTLs, jitter, and negative caching.
301 is permanent and browser-cached, saving load but hiding clicks. 302 is temporary, keeps analytics and edits working.
Emit a click event to a queue, aggregate in batches, write totals. Counts lag by seconds but redirects stay fast.
100M links/month is about 40 writes/s; at 100:1 reads are about 4,000/s average, 12,000 at a 3x peak. 5 years is about 3 TB.

lab.prompt: You are the engineer for a shortener expecting 100 million new links per month and 100 redirects per link. Produce a design: API, key generation, storage, redirect path with caching, and analytics. Defend each choice with a number.
requirements: Compute average and peak writes per second and redirects per second, stating your peak factor
Pick a key length and show the key space is large enough for 5 years
Describe how the create path makes keys unique across many servers
Describe the redirect path including cache hit and miss behaviour and TTLs
Choose 301 or 302 and justify it against analytics and edit needs
Describe how click counts are collected without slowing redirects
Explain what happens when the cache is empty and one mitigation
hints: 100M per month divided by about 2.6M seconds per month is roughly 40 per second
Total rows after 5 years times bytes per row gives storage; compare with one server's disk
Think about what a lost ID block costs: almost nothing
Estimate what fraction of keys is hot, multiply by bytes per entry, and compare with one cache node's RAM
Ask whether the counts must be exact in real time or can lag a few seconds
checklist: Traffic estimates are stated with assumptions
Key space is larger than total links needed
No two servers can issue the same key
Redirect reads check the cache before the database
Analytics writes are not on the redirect critical path
A cold-cache or expired-key failure case is addressed
